name: Silk'n Infinity / Flash&Go

card.summary: Silk'n home light-based hair-removal devices; an early small study of the brand's home pulsed light device reported hair reduction.
card.note: Study data are for an early Silk'n device, not necessarily these models.

quick.overview:
Silk'n makes home light-based hair-removal devices, including the Infinity and Flash&Go lines. They use low-energy pulsed light designed for self-treatment.

A 2009 study of an early Silk'n home pulsed light device tested 34 people and 92 sites with blinded hair counts. Sources on the Infinity and Flash&Go models themselves were not found.
quick.mechanism: Home pulsed light is absorbed by hair melanin, heating the follicle. Silk'n devices are described as small, light, low-energy and low-cost IPL systems.
quick.risks: A 2010 review of home IPL devices noted they are designed to cause biological damage to follicles, with eye safety a key design concern. Home-use IPL is generally considered less suited to very dark skin or light hair.

lead: Silk'n is a brand of home light-based hair-removal devices, including the Infinity and Flash&Go models, made by the Israeli company HomeSkinovations. People use them to reduce hair on the face, body and underarms, with the aim of smoother, hair-free skin without repeated salon or clinic visits [1][6]. In looksmaxxing and grooming culture, hair reduction is one of the routine ways people try to change how skin and facial areas look, from the beard line and neck to the body.

The devices use broad-spectrum pulsed light. Light is absorbed by the pigment in the hair, heating the follicle so that the hair is shed and, over a series of sessions, regrows less [5]. A 2009 study described an early Silk'n device as a small, light-weight, low-energy, low-cost IPL system for home use [1]. The brand has also made a blue-light device for acne, the Silk'n Blue [3].

The 2009 study tested the device on 34 people and 92 sites, with self-treatment supervised in clinic and hair counts done by a blinded observer [1]. A 2023 comparison of a Silk'n Flash&Go Lux home device with a professional diode laser in 15 women reported smaller hair reduction at home than with the professional laser [6]. No published trial specific to the Infinity model was found.

paras: Silk'n makes handheld flash devices for use at home. In the published literature the brand's devices appear as 'Silk'n', 'SensEpil' and 'Flash and Go' products from HomeSkinovations [1][2][6]. The Flash&Go Lux home device studied in 2023 emits light of 475 to 1200 nm [6].

Home IPL devices are designed to be cost-effective to mass-produce, easy to use without training, clinically effective and eye-safe, which are the engineering constraints listed in a 2010 review of home devices [2]. The same review notes that each of three leading home IPL products it examined, including Silk'n/SensEpil, relied on a mechanical or electrical safety feature that requires the aperture to be in contact with skin to prevent accidental eye exposure [2].

Intense pulsed light systems use a flashlamp producing brief pulses of broad-spectrum light, about 400 to 1200 nm, that is not coherent, unlike a laser [5]. Light is absorbed by chromophores such as melanin, hemoglobin and water; the absorbing structure is heated and the body clears the damage, a principle called selective photothermolysis [5]. In hair removal, melanin in the hair shaft and follicle absorbs the light, and the heat damages the follicle, including the papilla that produces hair [5].

Only follicles in the active growth phase respond at a given time, so treatment is repeated as other follicles enter that phase. Reference sources describe about 8 to 10 sessions, 4 to 6 weeks apart, for professional IPL, with no standard protocol and results depending on device and skin type [5]. IPL reduces hair counts rather than removing all hair, and it works best on darker, coarser hair [5].

A professional IPL study compared with alexandrite and diode lasers is summarized by Wikipedia: six-month reduction was about 67 percent for IPL, 69 percent for alexandrite and 72 percent for diode, a difference that was not statistically significant, although IPL is generally considered less effective than laser hair removal [5].

In the 2023 PLoS One study of 15 women, each received six axillary treatments at two to four week intervals with either a professional diode laser or the Silk'n Flash&Go Lux home device, with photographs and hair counts taken before each treatment and at a three-week follow-up. The professional laser showed overall reduction of 85 percent on the right axilla and 88 percent on the left; the home device showed 52 percent on the right and 46.3 percent on the left. Side effects were mild with both devices, and no serious adverse effects were reported [6].

Hair color and skin tone matter for light-based removal. Reference sources describe the best results on dark, coarse hair, with poor results on white, grey, light blonde and red hair, and the best outcomes on light skin with dark hair [5][7].

A 2009 study of the Silk'n home pulsed light device in 34 people and 92 test sites used pre- and post-treatment hair counts analysed by a blinded observer; participants performed the treatment themselves in clinic under supervision from an experienced laser hair removal nurse [1].

A 2014 IRB-approved study of 17 subjects examined the separate Silk'n Blue device for inflammatory acne, with eight treatments over four weeks and follow-up at one and three months. It reported a statistically significant decrease in mean acne counts from baseline (p=0.002) and in percent reduction (p=0.041), complete clearance in 36.4 percent of patients, full understanding of the device label in all patients, and no adverse events. The device has 24 LEDs emitting 405 to 460 nm [3].
A 2023 study compared the Silk'n Flash&Go Lux home device with a professional diode laser in 15 women (summarized above) [6]. No published trial specific to the Infinity model was found.

A 2010 review of home-use IPL devices stated that such systems are designed to cause biological damage to follicular structures, so precautions to prevent both ocular and epidermal damage are central to their design, and that there were then no dedicated international standards for IPL devices. It measured ocular hazard for three leading products against the IEC TR 60825-9 standard [2].

Reference sources list hyperpigmentation among IPL complications, and note that IPL and laser devices are described by manufacturers as suited to light to medium skin tones; photosensitizing medications and existing skin damage are described as contraindications, and the area should be shaved and free of sunburn [5]. Laser hair removal sources list burns, skin discoloration, hypopigmentation and infection among the serious risks of professional treatment [7].

Home IPL and laser hair-removal devices have expanded as a consumer market. Regulation varies by jurisdiction, and the 2010 review noted the absence of dedicated international standards for IPL devices [2]. Wikipedia reports that, as of 2025, the FDA had cleared two diode devices for over-the-counter sale, the Epilaser and the TRIA, and that the term 'permanent hair reduction' as cleared by the FDA in 1997 refers to a lasting reduction in regrowth, not total removal [7]. Practitioner licensing for professional services is regulated by US states [7].

Laser hair removal itself was tested for about 20 years before commercial release in 1995 to 1996, after researchers R. Rox Anderson and Melanie Grossman showed that a chromophore could be selectively targeted to damage follicle stem cells [7].

timeline.event: Commercial laser hair removal begins after about 20 years of experimental work.[7]
FDA approves the approach for 'permanent hair reduction'.[7]

angle.text: People use home pulsed-light devices to thin or reduce unwanted body and facial hair at home in place of repeated shaving, waxing or clinic visits. Studies of Silk'n devices measured hair counts before and after a series of sessions.
